# Vulnerability details

## Impact
All non-native assets (ERC20 tokens, NFTs, etc.) can be stolen by anyone from a `VirtualAccount` using its [payableCall(...)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/VirtualAccount.sol#L84-L112) method, which lacks the necessary access control modifier [requiresApprovedCaller](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/VirtualAccount.sol#L159-L167). See also, the [call(...)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/VirtualAccount.sol#L65-L82) method which utilizes the [requiresApprovedCaller](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/VirtualAccount.sol#L159-L167) modifier.  
Therefore, an attacker can craft a call to e.g. `ERC20.transfer(...)` on behalf of the contract, like the [withdrawERC20(...)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/VirtualAccount.sol#L55-L58) method does, while bypassing access control by executing the call via [payableCall(...)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/VirtualAccount.sol#L84-L112).  

As a consequence, all non-native assets of the `VirtualAccount` can be stolen by anyone causing a loss for its owner.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/c0dc3550e0754571b82d7bfd8f0282ac8fa5e42f/src/RootBridgeAgent.sol#L32


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The issue is, some ERC20 underlying tokens could have different decimals on other chains. For example, USDC in BNB chain has 18 decimals where it has 6 decimals in other chains such as Ethereum, Polygon ...etc. The root chain doesn't account for decimals changes across chains. An attacker could bridge a small amount of an underlying token (e.g. USDC) and claim it on the destination chain way much bigger. For example, in the case of USDC, 100 USDC deposited on BNB will turn into 100_000_000_000_000 USDC because of the big difference in decimals. This also impacts Innocent users who deposit the other way around (e.g. from Polygon to BNB), 100 USDC will turn into 0.00000000010000000 causing loss of funds to the user.

Note: according to the sponsor, there is not official list yet for chains that will be used since it has to pass governance first but some alt L1s and major L2s are expected to be used. So it is a variable list of chains and BNB (or even other not very popular chains) could possibly be included.

## Proof of Concept

In Maia, hToken is a mirror of its underlying token. hTokens has the same decimals as their underlying tokens. When a deposit from **chain A** to  **chain B** occurs, the same amount (hToken amount) and deposit (underlying token amount) are passed. **Chain B** assumes that the decimals on **chain A** are the same on **chain B** for the same underlying token, so it proceeds accordingly which open the vulnerability above for some ERC20 tokens.

Examples of underlying tokens:

- **on Polygon: 6 decimals**

- **on BNB: 18 decimals**
https://bscscan.com/token/0x8ac76a51cc950d9822d68b83fe1ad97b32cd580d

### USDT
- **on Polygon: 6 decimals**

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L578-L584


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Maia gets it's cross chain messaging primitives through Layer Zero. To get the price estimate, it uses the DstConfig price structure provided in RelayerV2 LZ: https://github.com/LayerZero-Labs/LayerZero/blob/main/contracts/RelayerV2.sol#L133.

The problem is that the important configuration parameters baseGas and gasPerByte, which are used to calculate the custom gas amount for the destination LZ message, use the values coming from the source chain. This is in contrast to LZ, which processes DstConfig against the ChainID key. The encoded amount of gas is described here: https://layerzero.gitbook.io/docs/guides/advanced/relayer-adapter-parameters.

## Proof of Concept
As a result, when these fields differ across chains, one of two things can happen:

Less serious - we waste extra gas, which is returned to the caller of lzReceive() (zero level).
More seriously, we underestimate the shipping cost, causing lzReceive() to return.
However, one implementation of the lzReceive() function does not handle lzReceive failure:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L578-L584.

The above-mentioned vulnerability in this case can lead to the loss of funds when transmitting an inter-chain message.

Manual review

Use target gas costs.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In RootBridgeAgentFactory, the privileged function createBridgeAgent() is lacking access control, which allows anyone to deploy a new RootBridgeAgent. Leveraging that, the attacker can inject malicious RootRouter and BranchRouter that can be used to trigger a reentrancy.

## Proof of Concept

The issue occurs in the createBridgeAgent function below:

    function createBridgeAgent(address _newRootRouterAddress) external returns (address newBridgeAgent) {
        newBridgeAgent = address(
            new RootBridgeAgent(
                rootChainId, 
                lzEndpointAddress, 
                rootPortAddress, 
                _newRootRouterAddress
            )
        );

        IRootPort(rootPortAddress).addBridgeAgent(msg.sender, newBridgeAgent);
    }
}


As we can see the function does not have any access control (modifier or check on the msg.sender). So any user can call it and add a new bridge agent.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add access control to RootBridgeAgentFactory.createBridgeAgent()


## Assessed type

Access Control

The vulnerability in the code of [ArbitrumBranchBridgeAgent.sol at line 89](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/ArbitrumBranchBridgeAgent.sol#L89) that the `_requiresEndpoint` modifier is not applied to the `retrySettlement` function. The impact of this vulnerability is high, as it could allow an attacker to steal a large amount of funds.

To fix this vulnerability, the `_requiresEndpoint` modifier should be added to the `retrySettlement` function. This will ensure that only the Root Bridge Agent can call the `retrySettlement` function.

## Proof of Concept
The function retrySettlement:
```solidity
    function retrySettlement(uint32, bytes calldata, GasParams[2] calldata, bool) external payable override lock {}

```


## Tools Used
VSCode

Here is the fixed code:
```solidity
    /// @inheritdoc IBranchBridgeAgent
    /// @dev This functionality should be accessed from Root environment
    function retrySettlement(uint32, bytes calldata, GasParams[2] calldata, bool) external payable override lock {
        _requiresEndpoint(msg.sender, msg.data);
    }

```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In contrast to OpenZeppelin, the Solmate's `SafeTransferLib` does not check for token contract's existence.
This behavior is expected and even straightforwardly pointed out in the source code: https://github.com/transmissions11/solmate/blob/547d98b09eac04f4bf8fe0fc65a63147e99c2748/src/utils/SafeTransferLib.sol#L9

The provided code-base uses `safeTransferFrom` in multiple of places during the bridging out - without verifying first, if token contract's exist.

In particular, it's became popular for protocols to deploy token in multiple networks with the same deploying address, to ensure a consistent token address across different networks.

E.g. 1INCH has got the same token address on Ethereum and BSC, and GEL token has the same address on Ethereum, Fantom and Polygon. There are other protocols have same contract addresses across different chains.

Taking into consideration that protocol is dedicated for cross-chain usage - system needs to ensure that token exists on the chain while performing `safeTransferFrom`.

Tokens can be transferred between different chains - thus ability to verify that token really exists on the chain is mandatory. Whenever `safeTransferFrom` executes without checking contract's existence - the transfer of empty token's address will succeed silently, without guarantee that  the underlying token has been sent.

> A trusted remote is the 40 bytes (for evm-to-evm messaging) that identifies another contract which you will receive messages from within your LayerZero User Application contract. The 40 bytes object is the packed bytes of the  remoteAddress + localAddress

the general call flow is:

a user send a message from source chain to dest chain

when send a messsage from [source chain](https://etherscan.io/address/0x66A71Dcef29A0fFBDBE3c6a460a3B5BC225Cd675#code#F1#L92), this method is called on layerzero endpoint

when the message is delivered on dest chain, the relayer is [calling this function](https://etherscan.io/address/0x66A71Dcef29A0fFBDBE3c6a460a3B5BC225Cd675#code#F1#L100) to deliver the message


There is a subtle difference between the implementation of solady (solmate’s) SafeTransferLib and OZ’s SafeERC20: OZ’s SafeERC20 checks if the token is a contract or not, solady’s SafeTransferLib does not. (it's based on solmate safetransferlib)

As a result, when the token’s address has no code, the transaction will just succeed with no error.
This attack vector was made well-known by the [qBridge hack back in Jan 2022](https://www.halborn.com/blog/post/explained-the-qubit-hack-january-2022).

It’s becoming popular for protocols to deploy their token across multiple networks and when they do so, a common practice is to deploy the token contract from the same deployer address and with the same nonce so that the token address can be the same for all the networks.

A sophisticated attacker can exploit it by taking advantage of that and setting traps on multiple potential tokens to create fake deposits. For example: 1INCH is using the same token address for both Ethereum and BSC; Gelato's $GEL token is using the same token address for Ethereum, Fantom and Polygon. **The key issue is that _setup is set to false on the first call to initialize in the constructor, but there is no check for _setup == false on subsequent calls.**

```Solidity
On the first call, _setup is true, so it passes the require check. _setup is then set to false. However, on subsequent calls, _setup will be false already, so the require check does not prevent re-initialization.

**The relevant code sections are:**

// Initial state
bool internal _setup;

  bridgeAgentAddress = _bridgeAgentAddress;
  bridgeAgentExecutorAddress = _hTokenFactory;
  
}


**On the first call:**

- _setup is true by default
- The require passes
- _setup is set to false
- State is initialized

**On a subsequent call:**

- _setup is already false from the first call
- The require check DOES NOT fail, since it checks if _setup == true
- _setup gets set to false again, which is a no-op
- State can be re-initialized by the attacker

This means an attacker can call initialize() again to re-initialize the contract's state with malicious values.

**Specifically, the attacker could:**

- Call initialize() the first time during normal setup
- Call initialize() again with their own bridgeAgentAddress and hTokenFactoryAddress
- Now the attacker controls critical contract state like where tokens are minted
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The depositToPort` and `withdrawFromPort` functions in `ArbitrumBridgePort.sol` do not properly validate that the `_depositor` and `_recipient` addresses are the same when transferring funds.

Specifically, in depositToPort:
Tokens are transferred from _depositor to the contract
New tokens are minted to _recipient
There is no check that _recipient == _depositor

In withdrawFromPort:
Tokens are burned from _depositor
Unlocked tokens are transferred to _recipient
Again no check that _recipient == _depositor

This vulnerability can lead to loss of funds. An attacker can drain tokens from a victim's account by setting the victim's address as _depositor but specifying their own address as _recipient in depositToPort and withdrawFromPort.


## Proof of Concept
To exploit the lack of _depositor and _recipient validation in depositToPort:
1. Attacker calls depositToPort()
2. Attacker sets parameters:
* _depositor = victimAddress
* _recipient = attackerAddress
* _underlyingAddress = tokenToSteal
* _depositAmount = amountToSteal
3. depositToPort transfers _depositAmount tokens from victimAddress to the contract
4. depositToPort mints new tokens to attackerAddress


## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Proper validation should be added to `require _depositor == _recipient` in both functions before transferring any funds. This will prevent the ability to improperly redirect transfers between accounts.
